analysis.one_liner: Bans hiring permanent strikebreakers for eight weeks of a strike but requires unions to win a secret-ballot strike vote first.
analysis.headline: The bill never left a House subcommittee: it was introduced in June 1991, referred to the Labor-Management Relations subcommittee in July, and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During an economic strike, employers can currently hire permanent replacements for striking workers at any time. This bill would make that an unfair labor practice for the first eight weeks of a strike, with exceptions for workers who engaged in violence or found equivalent jobs. It would also let strikers vote in union elections for 18 months instead of 12, and it would make it illegal for a union to call an economic strike unless a majority of employees in the bargaining unit vote for one by secret ballot. Finally, it urges the labor board to fast-track cases about reinstating permanently replaced strikers.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who go on economic strike would gain the most: for eight weeks their jobs could not be permanently filled, giving them real leverage at the bargaining table. Strikers who lose reinstatement rights would keep their union-election voting rights for 18 months instead of 12, and the NLRB would be urged to speed up their reinstatement cases. Rank-and-file union members would also gain a say, since union leadership could not call a strike without a majority secret-ballot vote.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Striking workers and rank-and-file union members

how_it_helps.text: Makes it an unfair labor practice for an employer to hire or threaten to hire permanent replacement workers during the first eight weeks of an economic strike, except for strikers who engage in violence or who find equivalent jobs elsewhere [S2][S3].
Extends from 12 to 18 months the period after a strike begins during which strikers not entitled to reinstatement can still vote in union representation elections [S2][S3].
Declares that the National Labor Relations Board should give first priority to processing unfair labor practice cases involving reinstatement of permanently replaced strikers [S2][S3].
Adds a new unfair labor practice for unions: calling an economic strike unless a simple majority of employees voting in the bargaining unit approve it by secret ballot [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers facing strikes would bear the main cost: for eight weeks they could not permanently staff struck jobs, limiting a tool they currently have to keep operating and pressure strikers. Union leadership would bear a different cost, since it could no longer call an economic strike on its own authority. Businesses would also face faster processing of striker reinstatement cases.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers facing strikes and union leadership

drawbacks.text: The secret-ballot strike-vote requirement would make strikes harder to call and slower to launch, since a union could not respond quickly to a breakdown in bargaining without first running an election [S2][S3].

An eight-week replacement ban is a partial protection only: after eight weeks, employers could again permanently replace strikers, and the exception for strikers who found 'equivalent employment' could be disputed in individual cases [S2][S3].
The NLRB speed provision is a statement of congressional opinion, not an enforceable rule, so it offers no guaranteed benefit [S2][S3].

Banning replacement hiring for eight weeks imposes real costs on employers who must keep customers and operations running during a strike, and some of those costs can be passed to workers and consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a genuine trade rather than a one-sided measure. Striking workers get a real but temporary shield against permanent replacement, and rank-and-file members get more control over strike decisions; in exchange, unions lose unilateral strike authority and employers face a shorter, but real, restriction on a classic counter-weapon. Neither the worker protection nor the strike-vote requirement is as strong as what either side's preferred legislation would have provided, which is consistent with the bill functioning as a compromise package. Because it never received any committee action, voters never got to see whether that trade had support.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Education and Labor Committee, then to its Labor-Management Relations subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative William Goodling, a Pennsylvania Republican, introduced the bill on June 12, 1991, joined by six Republican cosponsors including Ridge, Roukema, Gunderson, Houghton, and Regula [S1][S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and Labor the day it was introduced [S1][S5].
On July 11, 1991, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations, and no further action was recorded for the rest of the Congress [S1][S5].
The bill never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or Senate action, and expired when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers retained their ability to permanently replace economic strikers without any eight-week restriction, and union leadership avoided a new secret-ballot requirement before calling strikes. Striking workers gained nothing; the protections and the union-democracy requirement both died together.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers; unions; striking workers gained nothing

for.name: Rep. William F. Goodling
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its lead sponsor.

for.name: Reps. Ridge, Roukema, Gunderson, Houghton, and Regula
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral, passed it to its Labor-Management Relations subcommittee on July 11, 1991, and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: All seven House sponsors were Republicans; the Democratic-controlled House committee never took the bill up, and no Democratic support appears in the record [S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill bars them from hiring permanent replacements for eight weeks of an economic strike, removing a tool to keep operations running and to pressure strikers. This restriction is what gives striking workers bargaining leverage.

Union leaders would lose the power to call an economic strike without a majority secret-ballot vote, a real restriction on union authority. Striking union members, however, gain extended voting rights and a shield against replacement.
The eight-week ban would eliminate demand for permanent replacement hires during the early phase of economic strikes.
